                                        PROJECT NO. 58482

        LARGE LOAD DEMAND                             §            BEFORE THE
        MANAGEMENT SERVICE                            §     PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
                                                      §              OF TEXAS

     ERCOT STEEL MILLS’ COMMENTS REGARDING PROPOSED NEW RULE
        16 TAC §25.521, LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE

        The ERCOT Steel Mills1 offer the following comments and recommendations on the
proposal for publication of new §25.521 relating to Large Load Demand Management Service
(LLDMS), and responses to the specific questions posed by the Commission.

I.      INTRODUCTION

        The ERCOT Steel Mills strongly support effective demand response in the ERCOT
region. These comments are offered in support of a workable Large Load Demand Management
Service that can attract meaningful participation from qualifying large loads and provide ERCOT
with a reliable resource at a reasonable cost when needed.
        The Steel Mills have two interests in this proceeding: reliability and affordability. As for
reliability, load growth in ERCOT is projected to outpace the resources available to serve it, and
the Legislature has recognized that a service that brings additional large loads into emergency
demand response adds capability the region will need. As for affordability, under proposed
subsection (f)(3), LLDMS costs are properly charged to load serving entities (LSEs) on a load
ratio share basis and flow through to customers, including the Steel Mills. As a result,
affordability is an important consideration for all consumers.
        The ERCOT Steel Mills believe the Commission has produced a sound framework and
appreciate that the proposed rule reflects consideration of the comments parties filed in response
to Staff’s March 23, 2026 questions, particularly in its posture toward broad participation, its use
of a clear program-participation test for eligibility, and its funding of the service through a
dedicated budget.
        The following comments describe four additional specific recommendations offered by
the ERCOT Steel Mills and then respond to the Commission’s questions.



1
 The ERCOT Steel Mills include CMC Steel Texas, Gerdau Long Steel North America, Nucor Steel-Texas, a
division of Nucor Corporation, and Steel Dynamics Southwest, LLC.


                                                                                                        1
 II.    ADDITIONAL RECOMMENDATIONS REGARDING THE PROPOSED RULE

       A.      The large load customer should be explicitly permitted under proposed
               subsection (c) to designate a specific portion of its load for participation in
               the LLDMS to the degree not ineligible (so long as the designated curtailable
               load collectively equals or exceeds 1 MW).
       Large load customers may have a wide variety of loads within their footprint and may
have portions of their load that they either do not want to have participate in the LLDMS or that
are otherwise ineligible. Dividing the large load for participation could be required for a variety
of reasons. As an example, a portion of a customer’s load may be dedicated to providing
ancillary services, but another portion is not. Second, a large load customer may participate in
another demand response service that has an obligation period that does not overlap with the
specific procurement period for LLDMS in a request for proposal (RFP). As another example, a
large load customer may have some operations that can be curtailed and others that cannot or that
the customer does not wish to offer for curtailment. In these cases, large load customers should
be able to designate a portion of their load that is not ineligible to participate in the LLDMS.
Only the portion of those loads that are ineligible would be excluded, and the rest would be
eligible to participate at the customer’s election. This proposal would support reliability by
increasing the number of large load customers and the amount of load eligible to participate in
the LLMDS.

       B.      The 24-hour notice required by subsection (e)(1) should be notice of an actual
               deployment.

       Proposed subsection (e)(1) requires ERCOT to provide at least 24 hours’ notice to a
qualified scheduling entity (QSE) that a large load customer it represents “may be deployed to
reduce its load during the LLDMS obligation period” (emphasis added). This use of “may be”
rather than “will be” deployed makes this proposed program problematic for large load
customers who require up to 24 hours to shut down safely.
       Without a clear and certain notice of deployment, a participant would be left to speculate
on the fate of the deployment in 24 hours. A participant anticipating deployment will likely need
to begin ramping down in advance. If ERCOT ultimately does not deploy the participant, it may
have taken a facility offline unnecessarily, resulting in a substantial loss of production, restart
costs, and inadequate compensation. On the other hand, a participant who waits for certainty



                                                                                                      2
 faces the opposite risk. If a participant does not begin shutting down upon receiving the “may
be” notice, it may be unable to comply with a later directive to deploy from ERCOT. In that case,
the participant could face reduced payment, clawback penalties, or suspension for failing to
perform. Either outcome would make continued participation in the program less likely.
       The Steel Mills recommend that the Commission clarify that the 24-hour notice required
by subsection (e)(1) is notice of a deployment instruction rather than notice that a deployment
“may” occur. The Steel Mills further recommend that, in such cases where a 24-hour notice of
deployment requirement is not met, payments would be based on proportional performance and
no suspension or penalty under subsection (g) should apply.

       C.      Subsection (e)(3) should be clarified so that a participant held beyond its
               obligation period should be fairly compensated.
       Proposed subsection (e)(3) requires a deployed large load customer to remain deployed
“(A) for the duration of the EEA event; or (B) until the large load customer can be recalled
safely, as determined and communicated by ERCOT.” The provision is unclear as to whether the
deployment obligation ends upon the earlier of those two conditions or whether subsection (B)
governs in all cases. It is also unclear whether “recalled safely” requires an actual recall
instruction from ERCOT or merely ERCOT’s determination that a safe recall is possible, and
when ERCOT must communicate that determination to the participant.
       The Steel Mills recommend that the Commission resolve these issues in the rule or the
order adopting it so that participants can better understand their obligations.
       Furthermore, if ERCOT requires additional curtailment beyond a participant’s LLDMS
obligation period, the Steel Mills recommend that ERCOT extend its coverage by conducting
further procurement rather than holding a participant beyond its commitment. If ERCOT
nevertheless requires a participant to remain curtailed beyond the end of its obligation period,
ERCOT should adequately compensate the participant for that additional deployment time.

       D.      Subsection (f)(3) should allocate the costs of deployment and availability
               payments based on the period for which each service was rendered.
       Proposed subsection (f)(3) directs ERCOT to charge each LSE for LLDMS deployment
costs based upon the LSE’s load ratio share during the procurement period. We support this
concept. However, the section could be clarified as to how ERCOT recovers the cost of



                                                                                                   3
 availability payments made under subsection (f)(1)(C) to a participant that is procured but never
instructed to deploy.
       The ERCOT Steel Mills recommend that the cost of deployment payments be allocated
on load ratio share over the period during which the deployment occurs, and that the cost of
availability payments be allocated on load ratio share over the obligation period. This approach
reflects cost causation by assigning each cost to the load whose consumption during the relevant
period caused ERCOT to procure the service.

III.   RESPONSE TO COMMISSION QUESTIONS

       The ERCOT Steel Mills respond below to the specific questions posed by the
Commission.

       1.      Proposed subsection (f)(1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling
               entity representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT to
               deploy but is subject to availability verification during the Large Load Demand
               Management Service (LLDMS) obligation period. Should a large load customer
               that is available but not ultimately instructed to deploy during the LLDMS
               obligation period be compensated some percentage of the market clearing price
               for the large load customer’s availability to reduce demand during the LLDMS
               obligation period? If so, what is an appropriate payment to the large load
               customer for their availability during the LLDMS obligation period?
       Yes, a large load customer that is available but not deployed should still be compensated
for its availability. A large load participant whose offer is accepted and that holds capacity
available through the obligation period incurs real costs even if ERCOT never issues a
deployment instruction. Those costs can include schedule changes, plant preparation, and other
operational measures required to remain prepared for a potential shutdown on 24 hours’ notice.
The more directly the program compensates participants for those costs, the more likely large
load customers are to participate and submit competitive bids.
       As to the level of compensation for availability without deployment, the ERCOT Steel
Mills can support a figure higher than the proposed 25 percent. However, in this proceeding, the
25 percent may make sense for now as a starting level of compensation. The Commission may
not need to calibrate the percentage precisely, since the procurement is competitive and
participants will price the likelihood of deployment into their offers. If, after experience with




                                                                                                    4
 implementing the LLDMS program, this level does not produce participation at a level to attract
sufficient demand response, the Commission should reevaluate the percentage.
        The Steel Mills read subsection (f)(1)(C) to mean that the availability payment of 25
percent is calculated on the procured capacity across the full LLDMS obligation period. 2 The
Steel Mills support that structure. If the Commission adopts a lower percentage payment (e.g.,
25%) for availability than deployment, the ERCOT Steel Mills further recommend that, when a
deployment does not span the full obligation period, participants should be paid 100 percent of
the market clearing price for the deployment hours and 25 percent for the remaining hours of the
obligation period. A customer who is deployed for a short period will not adequately recover
their cost of curtailment and will be unlikely to enroll in the program or continue to participate.
This structure avoids the complexity of customer-specific minimum shutdown times
incorporated into the procurement process while retaining the ability for ERCOT to determine
the appropriate obligation period.

        2.       Proposed subsection (f)(4) imposes a maximum budget of $54 million in a
                 calendar year. What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?
        Without any experience yet under the LLDMS program, the ERCOT Steel Mills do not
know what an appropriate budget would be. That said, $54 million seems like a reasonable
starting point to begin with, subject to Commission review in the future.
        However, the Steel Mills think the ceiling would likely be insufficient without an
overflow budget provision, for at least two reasons. First, any ceiling will compel ERCOT to
provision an amount equal to the maximum deployment payment over any prospective LLDMS
procurement. For example, if ERCOT procures 16 hours’ worth of LLDMS, anticipating that
deployment would consume only a four-hour window within that obligation period, ERCOT
would expect to pay out the market clearing price × 4 hours (deployment cost) plus 25 percent of
the market clearing price × 12 hours (availability cost). In sum, ERCOT would expect to pay the
equivalent of the market clearing price × 7 hours. However, since ERCOT would be procuring
the option to deploy for the full 16 hours, ERCOT would likely need to budget for the market
clearing price × 16 hours (i.e., more than double the expected cost) in the event the emergency
event lasts for the entire obligation period in order to respect the budget ceiling. This additional

2
  Twenty-five percent “of the market clearing price” is a figure expressed in dollars per megawatt-hour, which
requires a megawatt-hour quantity, and the only period the subsection identifies is the LLDMS obligation period.


                                                                                                                   5
 headroom should be considered when setting a ceiling level and contemplating an overflow
mechanism.
        Second, the Steel Mills believe that if this program gets significant enrollment, a budget
of $54 million could be overwhelmed by a single extreme weather event like the recent Winter
Storm Fern. In preparation for such a storm, ERCOT might have procured LLDMS for an
obligation period of 96 hours.3 As explained in the previous paragraph, ERCOT would likely
need to allocate a sufficient portion of the budget for the full deployment potential of this service
(i.e., the full 96 hours). Figure 1 below shows the availability cost and the potential deployment
cost under various MW and bid levels. At the 1,000 MW procurement level and $1,000/MWh
market clearing price shown, full deployment would cost $96 million – nearly twice the ceiling.
Given the wide potential range of these assumption numbers and the potential for an overrun, a
ceiling of $54 million without an overflow provision risks underfunding this program, especially
with the possibility of multiple or extended emergency events.

    Figure 1: LLDMS Procurement Cost for a 96-hour period (Winter Storm Fern) vs. MW and
                                          $/MWh




        The Steel Mills recommend that the Commission consider raising the ceiling and provide
an overflow budget mechanism upon exhaustion of the original budget to support additional
procurements as determined by ERCOT. As an illustrative example of the mechanism: the
program’s initial annual budget is $X, and it may be increased during the year to $Y under Z




3
 https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/02/13/ERCOT-Monthly-January-2026-FINAL.pdf at 2: “Winter Storm
Fern, which occurred from January 23 through January 26.”


                                                                                                        6
 conditions. Some example conditions would be frequency or severity of events, enrollment
threshold, market clearing price threshold, or Commission directives.

       3.      What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and
               how far in advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?
       The ERCOT Steel Mills have no specific recommendations at this time but generally
support providing ERCOT flexibility to determine these program parameters consistent with the
rule and the intent of the statute to address severe weather events.

       4.      Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If
               so, what limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?
       Yes. ERCOT should be permitted to deploy LLDMS for any transmission event that
could reasonably lead to firm load shed. Firm load shed harms customers regardless of whether it
results from a generation shortfall during extreme weather or from a transmission constraint that
limits access to available generation in a particular location. Because grid emergencies often
have multiple contributing causes, demand reductions that help prevent firm load shed provide
value in either circumstance.

IV.    CONCLUSION

       The ERCOT Steel Mills support the creation of the Large Load Demand Management
Service and appreciate Staff’s work on the proposed rule. The recommendations above are
intended to help make the LLDMS a successful service that large loads can realistically
participate in and that ERCOT can rely on during an emergency. The Steel Mills respectfully
request that the Commission adopt these recommendations.




                                                                                                    7

Shenandoah, TX 77380

                                  EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

       The ERCOT Steel Mills offer the following comments and recommendations on the
proposed new rule 16 TAC §25.521 relating to Large Load Demand Management Service
(LLDMS).

Recommendations regarding the proposed rule
 • §25.521(c): Clarify that a large load customer may designate a specific portion of its load for
   participation in the LLDMS to the degree not ineligible (so long as the designated curtailable
   load collectively equals or exceeds 1 MW).
 • §25.521(e)(1): Clarify that the required 24-hour notice is notice by ERCOT of an actual
   deployment instruction, not notice that a large load customer “may be” deployed. Clarify
   further that, if ERCOT does not meet this notice requirement, payment should be
   proportional to performance and no penalty or suspension under subsection (g) should apply.
 • §25.521(e)(3): Resolve whether the deployment obligation ends at the earlier of the two
   conditions, whether “recalled safely” requires an actual recall instruction from ERCOT, and
   when that determination must be communicated. If the emergency conditions extend beyond
   the procured obligation period, ERCOT should conduct further procurement and adequately
   compensate participants for that additional time.
 • §25.521(f)(3): Allocate the cost of deployment payments on load ratio share over the period
   during which the deployment occurs, and the cost of availability payments on load ratio share
   over the obligation period.

Responses to the Commission’s questions
 • Question 1: To the degree a participant is available but not deployed, the large load should
   receive compensation for its availability. The Steel Mills believe the proposed 25 percent of
   the market clearing price is a reasonable starting place, subject to future Commission review
   after experience with the program.
 • Question 2: The $54 million ceiling is a reasonable place to start, but it should be paired
   with an overflow budget mechanism, and the Commission should evaluate whether the value
   should be increased after gaining experience with the program.
 • Question 3: No position.
 • Question 4: ERCOT should be permitted to deploy LLDMS for any transmission event that
   could reasonably lead to firm load shed.

       3.      What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and
               how far in advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?
       The ERCOT Steel Mills have no specific recommendations at this time but generally
support providing ERCOT flexibility to determine these program parameters consistent with the
rule and the intent of the statute to address severe weather events.

       4.      Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If
               so, what limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authorily?
       Yes. ERCOT should be permitted to deploy LLDMS for any transmission event that
could reasonably lead to firm load shed. Firm load shed harms customers regardless of whether it
results from a generation shortfall during extreme weather or from a transmission constraint that
limits access to available generation in a particular location. Because grid emergencies often
have multiple contributing causes, demand reductions that help prevent firm load shed provide
value in either circumstance.

IV.    CONCLUSION

       The ERCOT Steel Mills support the creation of the Large Load Demand Management
Service and appreciate Staff's work on the proposed rule. The recommendations above are
intended to help make the LLDMS a successful service that large loads can realistically
participate in and that ERCOT can rely on during an emergency. The Steel Mills respectfully
request that the Commission adopt these recommendations.

    ERCOT STEEL MILLS' COMMENTS REGARDING PROPOSED NEW RULE
       16 TAC §25.521, LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE

                                  EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

       The ERCOT Steel Mills offer the following comments and recommendations on the
proposed new rule 16 TAC §25.521 relating to Large Load Demand Management Service
(LLDMS).

Recommendations regarding the proposed rule
 • §25.521(c): Clarify that a large load customer may designate a specific portion of its load for
   participation in the LLDMS to the degree not ineligible (so long as the designated curtailable
   load collectively equals or exceeds 1 MW).

 • §25.521(e)(1): Clarify that the required 24-hour notice is notice by ERCOT of an actual
   deployment instruction, not notice that a large load customer "may be" deployed. Clarify
   further that, if ERCOT does not meet this notice requirement, payment should be
   proportional to performance and no penalty or suspension under subsection (g) should apply.
 • §25.521(e)(3): Resolve whether the deployment obligation ends at the earlier of the two
   conditions, whether "recalled safely" requires an actual recall instruction from ERCOT, and
   when that determination must be communicated. If the emergency conditions extend beyond
   the procured obligation period, ERCOT should conduct further procurement and adequately
   compensate participants for that additional time.
 • §25.521(f)(3): Allocate the cost of deployment payments on load ratio share over the period
   during which the deployment occurs, and the cost of availability payments on load ratio share
   over the obligation period.

Responses to the Commission's questions
 • Question 1: To the degree a participant is available but not deployed, the large load should
   receive compensation for its availability. The Steel Mills believe the proposed 25 percent of
   the market clearing price is a reasonable starting place, subject to future Commission review
   after experience with the program.
 • Question 2: The $54 million ceiling is a reasonable place to start, but it should be paired
   with an overflow budget mechanism, and the Commission should evaluate whether the value
   should be increased after gaining experience with the program.
 • Question 3: No position.

 • Question 4: ERCOT should be permitted to deploy LLDMS for any transmission event that
   could reasonably lead to firm load shed.
